title: Wilhelm cracks the ritual integration over the winter
notes: Wilhelm's winter work at Carrick: the folk system stops being spontaneous-only. He judges the formulaic-ritual step 'really easy — someone just needed to point it out'; the remaining work is formalizing the Artes Liberales / Philosophiae contribution.
source: Session recap 2026-07-25 (Ars Magica transcript), winter-1223 downtime.
body_text:
Wintering at **Carrick** while his research assistants are out gathering material, Wilhelm spends the season on **integration and research** — turning his folk system from a curiosity into something with proper mechanics.
**The breakthrough he's most confident about:** his current system knows only **spontaneous, ritual-style casting** (roll halved). Proper **formulaic** magic would let a caster add **Artes Liberales** and **Philosophiae** to the effort *and* drop the divide-by-two — roughly tripling the effective pool. Over the winter he works out that this ritual integration is, in his own estimate, **"really easy — someone just needed to point it out"**: give a caster the finished formula rather than making them improvise it each time.
**The Artes Liberales angle** is the part still taking his time: the obvious-once-said refinements a folk caster never bothered to name. If a ceremony wants a circle, it helps to know **geometry** enough to draw a true one; if it wants words of power, it helps to know **rhetoric** enough to project the voice. Formalizing how Artes Liberales and Philosophiae feed the working is the winter's real labor.
**Logistics.** His assistants are sent west and south to gather hedge-magic insight, carrying **sacks of grain and silver** as payment for anyone willing to teach the "easy stuff." Wilhelm writes letters — to the loose **wizard-circle** he keeps looped in on the project, to his family, and to **Dietrich** (his brother/scribe, back at his teaching post), whom he promises a **tractatus of the generated folk-magic spells** once it's finished. He intends to set up a **lab on shore** (he is chronically seasick and will not stay aboard ship an hour longer than he must), and has arranged for his research materials to be relocated from home toward wherever the covenant next bases itself. Feeds t019, t009, and the mundane vis-factory pitch (t020).

title: Foxglove fences the dragon's gold in London
notes: Auto-drafted from the 2026-08-08 session transcript; not yet owner-reviewed.
body_text: The Tide of Memory calls at London with trade out of Ghent. Foxglove — who took five bags of Tormente's hoard on impulse, with no plan — finds the gold near-worthless as spendable coin in a silver-standard economy. Through a fence she converts only a little (three coins), at a punishing one-for-one: a silver pound per gold piece, but legal tender at least. She keeps the bulk and, being wanted elsewhere, resolves to stay close to the covenant for cover while she holds it.

scene: Summer 1224 — a cove on the English coast
title: Llewellyn joins: Zeno's bargain and the time-crystal
notes: Auto-drafted from the 2026-08-08 session transcript; not yet owner-reviewed.
body_text:
Redcap messages sent from Ghent bring a reply at London: Llewellyn ex Miscellanea will meet the ship in a cove a fortnight on. He comes aboard for the northward leg, drawn by the promise of a Magic-aligned regio (Aquam-tinged) and “a safe place to catch my breath.”

On the voyage he confides his secret: captured by Zeno's paradox, he has extended his life by only ever living half his remaining span — a working grown so onerous, and maintained so long, that a sudden failure could be catastrophic. He hopes a regio of irregular time-flow will let him “catch the tide going out.” His time-quartz crystal, he says, reads those flows; Dagmar's cursory study finds it innately, naturally magical — a found object, not a made artifact, and not Llewellyn's own discovery.

scene: Summer 1224 — a cliff-cave northeast of York
title: The crown delivered: Mímormr freed
notes: Auto-drafted from the 2026-08-08 session transcript; not yet owner-reviewed.
body_text:
Meeting Valdemar's ship off Northumbria, Dagmar explains Tormente's quest, and the crew rows to a cliff-cave northeast of York, silver-shimmered within. The occupant is no drake like Tormente but a vast silver-and-aquamarine worm who names itself Mímormr, great-grandchild of Jörmungandr and a speaker with the bones of the dead — bound in the cave for ages by Tormente, who (it says) calls its ancestry false and its deeds wicked.

The crown proves a pardon: a name-release that undoes the binding. Mímormr takes it and emerges, freed. Offered a boon, Dagmar — through Valdemar, who parses the garbled speech with his Ansuz rune — asks only for a token to carry back to Tormente as proof the task is done. Mímormr reaches for Dagmar's mind, seemingly to leave a readable mark but in truth to crush his skull; Dagmar treats it as an attack, slips it with his Parma, and takes no effect — while Mímormr believes it succeeded. Told of a relative's bones basking in power out in the North Sea, it means to finish its work here and then make east to meet that ancestor, and climbs away into the countryside, loosed upon the world.

Examining the empty cave, the magi (Dagmar's premonitions; Valdemar and Llewellyn on the stone) find the binding was never Hermetic: a Muto-Terram-scale warping of the rock against its grain, plus an Adamic name-binding — power that would tax a trained magus to match.
